title: Coupling generative AI with 3D printing for historical building renovation: a case study of Lingnan stucco relief
abstract: Abstract The accelerating digitalization of the construction sector has brought into sharp focus the inefficiencies and labor-intensive nature inherent in traditional craftsmanship for historical architecture. In response, this study proposes an AI-driven generative design workflow that translates semantic inputs into 2D imagery and 3D models, enabling the systematic learning and replication of stylistic features from a quintessential southern Chinese architectural ornament—the Lingnan stucco relief. This approach moves beyond the conventional reliance on individual expertise and heuristic empirical methods. The structural performance of the AI-generated designs was evaluated through combined material testing and numerical simulations. Concurrently, hybrid additive manufacturing techniques were explored for rapid physical prototyping. Collectively, this integrated framework illustrates the feasibility of revitalizing traditional craft practices within a contemporary intelligent paradigm, offering a technological pathway for the preservation and renovation of historic built heritage.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Historical architecture stands as a tangible record of human civilization, encapsulating not only cultural and technological milestones but also the ingenuity of past societies. Embedded within each architectural heritage site is a constellation of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) elements, including design philosophies, construction systems, and material practices that are intrinsically tied to the restoration, renewal, and adaptive reuse of these structures (Vecco,  57 ). Yet, as modern society progresses, many of these ICH traditions have steadily lost their sustaining contexts, as contemporary technologies increasingly supplant conventional craft techniques, thereby threatening their continued transmission. Moreover, the structural and decorative components of historical buildings inevitably decay over time, compromising both their aesthetic integrity and functional performance, while the corresponding restoration methods often lag behind in efficacy and applicability. Hence, safeguarding the craft knowledge associated with historical architecture is as imperative as preserving the physical fabric of the buildings themselves.

Restoration of historic architecture is highly customized and largely reliant on the accumulated expertise of artisans. Consequently, such work is often labor-intensive and time-consuming, which in turn leads to greater energy consumption (Mazzarella,  35 ). In practice, however, these processes still heavily rely on the expertise and craftsmanship of artisans, making them inherently difficult to document and pass on to next-generation practitioners. Consequently, there is an emergent need for supplementary design and construction strategies that can support the renovation and renewal of traditional architectural ornamentation, particularly in contexts where strict adherence to heritage protocols is not mandatory. Such approaches could alleviate the pressures imposed by extended project timelines and the growing scarcity of skilled conservators.

Parallel to these challenges, the proliferation of computational tools has catalyzed a paradigm shift in architectural design and construction methodologies. Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin technologies are now exerting a profound influence on contemporary practice, with generative AI offering particularly promising avenues. These models, capable of producing original content, have drawn considerable attention in recent years. Large language models like ChatGPT have become enmeshed in human decision-making processes across diverse domains (Chang et al.,  7 ). Within the manufacturing sector, generative AI has demonstrated the capacity to compensate for shortages of highly trained technical personnel and master craftspeople (Ooi et al.,  40 ). By extension, these generative technologies hold considerable promise for the field of traditional architecture, especially in the documentation, reinterpretation, and restoration of historic architectural forms.

Additive manufacturing enables the production of highly customized products while simultaneously minimizing material waste, thereby reducing construction costs (Zhou et al.,  78 ). Evidently, additive manufacturing holds great promise in the cultural heritage sector (Balletti et al.,  1 ; Moga et al.,  36 ), particularly in the partial restoration of historic building components, including gypsum figures (Saha et al.,  51 ), wood (Rizzo et al.,  47 ), and rockery (Dong et al.,  10 ). These advanced design and fabrication techniques not only address the declining availability of skilled artisans in traditional craftsmanship but also enhance efficiency at restoration sites and expand the applications of cultural heritage conservation. Ultimately, a critical challenge lies in leveraging digitalization and intelligent technologies to establish an optimized restoration workflow that reduces costs and improves productivity.

In this study, we demonstrate a workflow that integrates AI-generated design, finite element method (FEM) analysis, and additive manufacturing to produce stylistic decorative components for historical buildings within a digitalized and rational framework. To validate its feasibility, our study selected a well-known local traditional craftsmanship example in Southern China, known as Lingnan stucco relief (pronounced as “Hui Su” in Chinese). With an aim of providing complementary intelligent methods to assist traditional craftsmanship within historical buildings, we established an initial mechanical model of stucco relief materials through experimental analysis and proposed an additive manufacturing based fabrication method for rapid prototyping and physical model production. Figure  1  showcases three major tasks presented in this work to preserve this regional cultural identity and to enable the reuse of ancient construction techniques. The core content of this work is presented in Sects.  4  and  5 . Section  4  introduces a generalized methodology for architectural heritage that encompasses generative design, material characterization, and additively manufactured prototyping. Section  5  then presents the detailed designs, analyses, and fabrications specific to the Lingnan stucco relief. In the design phase, we fine-tuned a Stable Diffusion model using a set of stucco relief images via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), enabling the generation of stucco relief style imagery. These images were subsequently transformed into three dimensional reliefs or reconstructed into 3D models with skeletal structures. In the analysis phase, finite element analysis was employed, informed by material tests, to construct a mechanical model of the stucco relief, facilitating structural analysis and guiding the construction process. During the construction phase, AI generated stucco relief prototypes were fabricated using multiple additive manufacturing methods, and the physical structures were built using 3D printed molds and supporting frameworks.
